new_note: *For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:13). *For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of Adam be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.* (Matthew 12:40). The Father holds both doors: he leads down to the gates of hell and he brings up again. Yahusha (Jesus) gave that generation one sign, the sign of Jonah — three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, and then up. The resurrection was not a new idea arriving in Galilee; the library already knew that the one who has power of life and death brings up from the grave, and the King walked that road in his own body so the sign would stand in front of everyone.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:13 — *you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* The sign of Jonah walks that road: three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, then up (Matthew 12:40).

new_note: *For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:13). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). The gates of hell have no final say, because the one who leads down to those gates is the same one who brings up again. That is what stands behind the promise to Peter: the assembly is built on the King who would be raised the third day (he says so plainly at verse 21), and the gates that closed on him could not hold him, so they will not prevail against what he builds. The same chapter opens with the sign of Jonah (verse 4); the whole chapter is carrying this one truth, that the grave is a door the Father opens.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:13 — *you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* The gates that could not hold the raised King will not prevail against his assembly (Matthew 16:18).

new_note: *A man indeed killeth through his malice: and the spirit, when it is gone forth, returns not; neither the soul received up comes again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:14). *But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.* (Matthew 9:25). The verse draws the line a man cannot cross: he can kill, but once the spirit has gone forth he cannot call it back. Then Yahusha (Jesus) takes a dead girl by the hand and she arises. What Wisdom of Solomon had just said belongs to Yahuah (God) alone — the power of life and death, leading down and bringing up again (16:13) — is done in a house in Capernaum by a man with his hand on a child. That is who he is: not the formless Father, but the one through whom the Father's power has always acted, now standing in flesh.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:14 — *the spirit, when it is gone forth, returns not.* What no man can do, the King does with his hand on a dead girl (Matthew 9:25).

new_note: *Instead of which you feddest your own people with angels’ food, and did send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and agreeing to every taste.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:20). *And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.* (Matthew 14:19). Bread from heaven, prepared without their labour, was how the Father fed his own people in the wilderness. On the grass in a desert place Yahusha (Jesus) looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and the loaves go out through the disciples' hands to a multitude that brought nothing but its hunger. The same hand that sent the manna is feeding Yashar'el (Israel) again, and John's account of this same meal ends with him saying who the bread is: *I am the bread of life* (John 6:35).
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:20 — *did send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour.* Bread without labour again, blessed and broken in a desert place and handed out by the disciples (Matthew 14:19).

new_note: *Instead of which you feddest your own people with angels’ food, and did send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and agreeing to every taste.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:20). *Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat.* (John 6:31). The crowd at Capernaum quotes the manna back at him as the high mark of what heaven has ever given. The library agrees with them about the manna: it was angels' food, sent from heaven without their labour, fitted to every taste. Yahusha (Jesus) does not take a word of it back; he says the Father who sent that bread is now giving the true bread, and the true bread is himself (John 6:32, 35). The manna was real and it was heaven's, and it was pointing past itself to the one who came down.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:20 — *you feddest your own people with angels’ food.* The crowd cites the same wilderness bread, *He gave them bread from heaven to eat* (John 6:31).

new_note: *For your sustenance declared your sweetness to your children, and serving to the appetite of the eater, tempered itself to every man’s liking.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:21). *For the bread of Elohim (God) is he which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life unto the world.* (John 6:33). The manna carried the Father's sweetness to his children and fitted itself to every one who ate it. John names the bread of Elohim (God) as a person — he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. The sweetness the wilderness tasted was a foretaste of the one who came down; the manna fed a generation, and the Bread who came down gives life.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:21 — *your sustenance declared your sweetness to your children.* The sweetness the wilderness tasted is the Bread who comes down and gives life to the world (John 6:33).

new_note: *That your children, O Yahuah (God), whom you lovest, might know, that it is not the growing of fruits that nourishes man: but that it is your word, which preserves them that put their trust in you.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:26). *And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the grass, and took the five loaves, and the two fishes, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake, and gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.* (Matthew 14:19). The manna was a lesson, and Wisdom of Solomon says what the lesson was: it is not the harvest that keeps a man alive but the word of Yahuah (God). When the King blesses five loaves and feeds a multitude, the loaves are the smaller thing; the disciples who hand them out have been receiving his word all along, and in John's telling of this same meal he says outright that his words are spirit and life (John 6:63). The bread points past itself to the word that preserves those who trust him.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:26 — *it is not the growing of fruits that nourishes man: but that it is your word.* The loaves blessed and broken point past themselves to the word that nourishes (Matthew 14:19).

new_note: *That your children, O Yahuah (God), whom you lovest, might know, that it is not the growing of fruits that nourishes man: but that it is your word, which preserves them that put their trust in you.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:26). *Then Yahusha (Jesus) said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven.* (John 6:32). The manna was teaching that it is the word of Yahuah (God), not the harvest, that keeps his children alive. Yahusha (Jesus) says Moses did not give the bread from heaven; the Father did, and the Father is now giving the true bread. The word that preserved the wilderness generation is standing in front of the crowd in flesh, the Word made flesh who is himself the bread. What the manna said in a picture, he says in person.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:26 — *it is your word, which preserves them that put their trust in you.* The word that preserved the wilderness is the true bread the Father now gives (John 6:32).

new_note: *Your Almighty word leaped down from heaven out of your royal throne, as a fierce man of war into the midst of a land of destruction,* (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15). *But straightway Yahusha (Jesus) spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.* (Matthew 14:27). The almighty word leaped down from the throne into Egypt's night as a man of war. In the fourth watch of another night the disciples see a figure on the sea and are terrified, and the Word speaks: it is I; be not afraid. The one who came down from the Father's throne on Passover night is the same one walking the dark water, the Word who was with Elohim (God) and was made flesh (John 1:1, 14). Wisdom of Solomon shows the Word as one who comes down and acts; Matthew shows him in flesh naming himself.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 18:15 — *Your Almighty word leaped down from heaven out of your royal throne.* The Word who came down on Passover night speaks across the dark water, *it is I; be not afraid* (Matthew 14:27).

new_note: *And brought your unfeigned commandment as a sharp sword, and standing up filled all things with death; and it touched the heaven, but it stood upon the earth.* (Wisdom of Solomon 18:16). *For the word of Elohim (God) is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.* (Hebrews 4:12). In Egypt the word came as a sharp sword that filled the land with death, touching heaven and standing on the earth. Hebrews says the same word is still a sword, sharper than any two-edged blade, and it now cuts where no Egyptian saw it fall — between soul and spirit, into the thoughts and intents of the heart. The sword is the same; the field it works has moved inward. The one who judged Egypt in a night reads the heart of the one who reads him.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 18:16 — *brought your unfeigned commandment as a sharp sword.* The same sword, now sharper than any twoedged sword and turned on the heart (Hebrews 4:12).

new_note: *And when he had called him, he said, My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother, but honour her all the days of your life, and do that which shall please her, and grieve her not.* (Tobit 4:3). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). A dying father in exile tells his son: honour your mother all the days of her life, please her, grieve her not. That is the fifth commandment lived out to the end of a parent's days, in a household far from the land. Yahusha (Jesus) quotes the same commandment against a tradition that let a man say *It is a gift* and so be freed from supporting his parents (15:5–6). Tobit shows what the commandment looks like when it is kept; the tradition shows what it looks like when a religious system finds a way around it, and it is the system that is being answered, not the people who were taught it.
member_note: Tobit 4:3 — *despise not your mother, but honour her all the days of your life.* The commandment to honour father and mother, kept to the end of her days, which the gift tradition voided (Matthew 15:4).

new_note: *And when he had called him, he said, My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother, but honour her all the days of your life, and do that which shall please her, and grieve her not.* (Tobit 4:3). *And he laid his hands on them, and departed thence.* (Matthew 19:15). Tobit calls his son to him before he dies and hands him the commandments — honour your mother, bury me, walk uprightly — which is a father's blessing in the old form. Parents brought their children to Yahusha (Jesus) and he laid his hands on them. The library shows a father passing covenant life to the next generation; the gospel shows the King receiving the children their parents bring to him. The two belong together at the household, where the covenant has always been handed down.
member_note: Tobit 4:3 — *My son, when I am dead, bury me; and despise not your mother.* A father handing covenant life to his son; the King laying hands on the children brought to him (Matthew 19:15).
flag: Thin pairing. The old note was mostly padding (Genesis 48, Numbers 6) around a weak link between Tobit 4:3 and Matthew 19:15; I kept the only real thread, a father blessing his son with instruction and parents bringing children to the King for blessing. Consider whether this card should stand at all.

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Give to the poor and turn your face from none, and the face of Yahuah (God) will not turn from you. That is the mercy Hosea asked for in place of sacrifice, the word Yahusha (Jesus) sends the Pharisees to go and learn. They were offended that he sat at table with sinners (9:11); Tobit had told his son not to turn his face from any poor man. Mercy toward the one in need is the heart of the Torah, and a system that keeps its credentials clean while turning its face away has lost the thing the commandment was for.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* The mercy Hosea asked for in place of sacrifice, which the Pharisees at the table had forgotten (Matthew 9:13).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.* (Matthew 25:40). Tobit promises that the face of Yahuah (God) stays turned toward the man who does not turn his face from the poor. Yahusha (Jesus) says it more sharply: what you did to the least of my brethren you did to me. The giver meets the King in the one he feeds, and the King's face toward him is the Father's face toward him. The same thing was said to Saul on the Damascus road, that to persecute the brethren was to persecute him (Acts 9:4–5). It is personal: mercy toward the King's brethren is mercy the King himself receives.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor.* The face not turned from the poor meets the King in the least of his brethren (Matthew 25:40).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms makes an atonement for sins.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:30). Two books of the library say one thing in two pictures. Tobit's open hand keeps the face of Yahuah (God) turned toward the giver; Sirach says alms put out sin the way water puts out fire. Neither is buying anything. Alms is mercy, mercy is what the Torah asks of a man, and the one who walks in it walks in the light of the Father's face.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor.* Sirach's picture of the same mercy: *alms makes an atonement for sins* as water quenches fire (Ecclesiasticus 3:30).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *And stretch yours hand to the poor, that your blessing may be perfected.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:32). Tobit tells his son to turn his face toward the poor; Sirach tells his to stretch out his hand to them so that his blessing may be perfected. The face and the hand together are the whole posture of the righteous man in the library: see the need and move toward it. The blessing is not finished until the hand is open.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor.* Sirach adds the hand to the face: *stretch yours hand to the poor, that your blessing may be perfected* (Ecclesiasticus 7:32).
flag: Live-text misprint in Ecclesiasticus 7:32: 'stretch yours hand' (should be 'your hand'). Quoted as it stands.

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *My son, blemish not your good deeds, neither use uncomfortable words when you give any thing.* (Ecclesiasticus 18:15). Tobit warns against the envious eye when giving; Sirach warns against the sour word. Both know that a gift can be spoiled by the spirit it comes in. The alms Yahuah (God) looks on is given gladly, without a grudging eye and without a hard word to the one who receives it.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *when you give alms, let not your eye be envious.* Sirach's twin warning, not to blemish the good deed with uncomfortable words (Ecclesiasticus 18:15).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *And the third I gave to them to whom it was meet, as Debora my father’s mother had commanded me, because I was left an orphan by my father.* (Tobit 1:8). Tobit 1:8 shows the old man doing as a young man what he later teaches: the third tithe given to those to whom it was meet, as his grandmother Debora had commanded him. Three generations carry it, Debora to Tobit, Tobit to Tobias. The alms he charges on his son in chapter 4 is a tithe he had been paying since he was an orphan.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor.* The charge to his son is the third tithe Tobit himself paid from his orphan years (Tobit 1:8).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *But she replied upon me, It was given for a gift more than the wages. Howbeit I did not believe her, but told her render it to the owners: and I was abashed at her. But she replied upon me, Where are your alms and your righteous deeds? behold, you and all your works are known.* (Tobit 2:14). Blind and poor, Tobit is mocked by his own wife: where are your alms and your righteous deeds now? He does not answer her reproach by giving up the practice. Two chapters later he hands the same practice to his son as the way to keep the face of Yahuah (God) toward him. The reproach did not move him, because alms were never a trade for comfort; they were covenant life, kept in blindness as in sight.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* The alms Anna threw in his face are the alms he charges on his son (Tobit 2:14).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you.* (Luke 11:41). The Pharisees were careful about the outside of the cup; Yahusha (Jesus) told them the cleansing they needed was to give alms of what they had. Tobit had told his son the same long before: give of what you have, turn your face from no poor man, and the face of Yahuah (God) stays toward you. The King is not inventing a new rule; he is pointing a religious system back to the mercy the library had been teaching every son.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor.* The alms that make all things clean (Luke 11:41) are the alms Tobit charged on his son.

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *Then the high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children:* (2 Maccabees 3:10). When Heliodorus came to seize the temple treasury, the high priest told him the money was laid up for widows and fatherless children. The temple was keeping what Tobit charged his son to give: the poor had a store in the house of Yahuah (God). The library shows alms as a private duty in Tobit and a public trust in Maccabees, and the same mercy stands behind both.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor.* The temple treasury kept money for widows and the fatherless, the same alms held in public trust (2 Maccabees 3:10).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you. If you have abundance give alms accordingly: if you have but a little, be not afraid to give according to that little:* (Tobit 4:7–8). *Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for Elohim (God) loveth a cheerful giver.* (2 Corinthians 9:7). Tobit's son is told to give without an envious eye, out of abundance or out of a little. Paul says the same to Corinth: not grudgingly, not of necessity, each as he purposes in his heart, for Elohim (God) loves a cheerful giver. The heart that gives gladly is the heart the library had been shaping for generations before the letter. Paul was not writing a new ethic for a new people; he was writing Tobit's charge to the scattered children of Yashar'el (Israel) who had grown up among the nations and forgotten it.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *when you give alms, let not your eye be envious.* Give of abundance or of little, without the envious eye; *not grudgingly, or of necessity* (2 Corinthians 9:7).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *If any man or woman that believeth have widows, let them relieve them, and let not the church be charged; that it may relieve them that are widows indeed.* (1 Timothy 5:16). Tobit's charge is to turn his face from no poor man. Paul orders the believing household to relieve its own widows, so that the assembly's care is kept for the widows who have no one. Both put the first duty of mercy at home, in the household, before it goes out the door. The face never turned from the poor begins with the poor who are nearest.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor.* The household relieves its own widows first (1 Timothy 5:16), the face never turned from the nearest poor.

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.* (Titus 3:14). Paul tells Titus to teach the believers a settled habit of usefulness: maintain good works for necessary uses, and so bear fruit. Tobit's charge is one of those works named exactly — give alms of what you have, turn your face from no poor man. This is the doing of mercy the Torah commands and the new heart loves, and the library had been teaching it to sons in exile long before Paul wrote to Crete.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor.* The good work for necessary uses that keeps the believer from being unfruitful (Titus 3:14).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.* (Exodus 22:21). Tobit lives in Nineveh, a stranger among the nations, and he teaches his son the open hand to the poor. The Torah had told Yashar'el (Israel) not to vex or oppress the stranger, because they had been strangers in Egypt. Tobit is now the stranger, and he keeps the commandment from the other side of it, showing mercy where he might have asked for it. The promise mirrors the warning: turn not your face from the poor, and Yahuah (God) turns not his from you.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* The stranger in Nineveh keeps the mercy Torah commanded toward the stranger (Exodus 22:21).

new_note: *Give alms of your substance; and when you give alms, let not your eye be envious, neither turn your face from any poor, and the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* (Tobit 4:7). *Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.* (Matthew 6:1). Tobit ties alms to one face, the face of Yahuah (God) turned toward the giver. Yahusha (Jesus) warns against alms done to be seen of men, because a gift aimed at men's eyes has already had its reward and the Father's is lost. Both are saying whose face the giver should be looking for. Tobit never mentions secrecy, but he sets the giver before the Father's face and no one else's, and that is the whole of the warning in Matthew.
member_note: Tobit 4:7 — *the face of Yahuah (God) shall not be turned away from you.* Alms given for the Father's face, not for men's eyes (Matthew 6:1).
flag: Corrected the old note: it called Tobit 4:7 'secret-handed giving', but the verse says nothing about secrecy. The real link is whose face the giver seeks (the Father's, not men's).

new_note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Alms laid up are a treasure against the day of need; Tobit sees the open hand as storing something before Yahuah (God). Yahusha (Jesus) tells the Pharisees to go learn Hosea's word, mercy and not sacrifice. They had stored up sacrifices and credentials; the heart of the Torah was the mercy Tobit's son was told to lay up. The treasure that counts in the day of necessity is the mercy that was done, and the King is calling a religious system back to it.
member_note: Tobit 4:9 — *you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* The treasure laid up by mercy, the thing Hosea asked for in place of sacrifice (Matthew 9:13).

new_note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). *Yahusha (Jesus) said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.* (Matthew 19:21). The young ruler asked what he still lacked, and the King told him: sell, give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven. Tobit had told his son the same thing long before — alms are a good treasure laid up against the day of necessity. The Torah already commanded the open hand to the poor brother, and the library carried it forward as treasure laid up. Yahusha (Jesus) was not raising the bar on the young man; he was reading him the library, and the young man went away sorrowful because he could not walk it.
member_note: Tobit 4:9 — *a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* Give to the poor and have treasure in heaven (Matthew 19:21), the treasure Tobit told his son to lay up.

new_note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). *Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.* (Luke 12:33). Tobit's charge to give alms comes with a reason: the giver is laying up a good treasure against the day of necessity. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same thing with a picture — sell, give alms, and you have bags that do not wear out, a treasure in the heavens that does not fail. What is given now is what is stored for then. The library names the treasure the open hand lays up; the gospel names where it is kept and why no thief or moth can reach it.
member_note: Tobit 4:9 — *a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* The alms given now are the bags that wax not old, the treasure that faileth not (Luke 12:33).

new_note: *For you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* (Tobit 4:9). *This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in Elohim (God) might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.* (Titus 3:8). Tobit's son is told to give alms as treasure laid up against the day of need, out of a heart that fears Yahuah (God) and keeps his commandments (4:5). Paul tells Titus to affirm constantly that those who have believed be careful to maintain good works, good and profitable to men. The two are one posture: believing and doing are not rivals, and the open hand is what a believing heart does. The library had been teaching that to sons in exile long before the letter.
member_note: Tobit 4:9 — *you layest up a good treasure for thyself against the day of necessity.* Alms as good works laid up, the fruit of a believing heart careful to maintain them (Titus 3:8).

new_note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:* (Matthew 6:20). Tobit tells his son that alms deliver from death and keep a man out of the darkness; the open hand protects the giver in the day of necessity. Yahusha (Jesus) says to lay up treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not corrupt and thieves do not break through. Both are talking about what cannot be lost. Tobit names the deliverance the open hand brings; the gospel names the storehouse the open hand fills, and nothing gets in to spoil it.
member_note: Tobit 4:10 — *alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* The deliverance the open hand brings, stored where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt (Matthew 6:20).

new_note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Tobit says alms deliver from death, and he says it in the voice of a father who has lived it. The Pharisees at Matthew's table had their sacrifices in order and their mercy withheld, and the King sent them to Hosea: mercy, and not sacrifice. Tobit had already named mercy as the thing that delivers. A religion that keeps its offerings and loses its mercy has kept the shell and lost the life.
member_note: Tobit 4:10 — *alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* Mercy is what delivers, and mercy is what Hosea asked for in place of sacrifice (Matthew 9:13).

new_note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.* (Matthew 12:7). Tobit gives mercy its full weight: alms deliver from death and keep a man from the darkness. Mercy is not the soft side of the Torah, something to be set aside when the rules get strict. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same to the Pharisees on the Sabbath: if you had known what Hosea meant by mercy and not sacrifice, you would not have condemned the guiltless. The system that condemned hungry disciples had lost the thing Tobit's household had kept, and the King names the loss in Hosea's own words.
member_note: Tobit 4:10 — *alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* Mercy carries eternal weight; the Sabbath condemnation showed a system that had lost it (Matthew 12:7).

new_note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.* (Luke 12:33). Tobit says alms deliver from death and keep the giver out of darkness; the open hand protects the one who opens it. Yahusha (Jesus) says to sell, give alms, and have a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth corrupts. Both are saying that what is given away is the one thing that cannot be taken away. The library names the deliverance; the gospel names the storehouse no thief can reach.
member_note: Tobit 4:10 — *alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* The open hand delivers from death; its treasure is in the heavens where no thief approacheth (Luke 12:33).

new_note: *Do that to no man which you hatest: drink not wine to make you drunken: neither let drunkenness go with you in your journey.* (Tobit 4:15). *Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.* (Matthew 7:12). Here is the golden rule in the Hebrew library, in its negative form, from a father to his son generations before the Sermon on the Mount. Yahusha (Jesus) states it positively and then says what it is: *this is the law and the prophets.* He was not bringing a kinder ethic to replace a Torah too hard to keep; he was naming the heart of the Torah that Tobit had already handed to his son. The teaching that the King invented a new religion in place of the law collapses against this one verse in Tobit.
member_note: Tobit 4:15 — *Do that to no man which you hatest.* The golden rule in negative form, generations before *this is the law and the prophets* (Matthew 7:12).
flag: Corrected the old note: it attributed Tobit 4:15 to 'the angel Raphael's closing instruction to Tobias'. Tobit 4 is Tobit the father instructing his son; Raphael's instruction is Tobit 12.

new_note: *Give of your bread to the hungry, and of your garments to them that are naked; and according to your abundance give alms: and let not your eye be envious, when you give alms.* (Tobit 4:16). *For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:* (Matthew 25:35). Bread to the hungry, garments to the naked, alms according to abundance, no envious eye — Tobit gives his son two of the very things the King names at the judgment: *I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat ... naked, and ye clothed me.* Isaiah had said the same, to deal bread to the hungry and cover the naked. This is not a charity program for the world in general; the King says it is mercy done to his brethren, and it is the measure by which the sheep are told from the goats. The library had been teaching that measure in the exile household all along.
member_note: Tobit 4:16 — *Give of your bread to the hungry, and of your garments to them that are naked.* Two of the King's own measures at the judgment, *I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat* (Matthew 25:35).

new_note: *You madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay: of them came mankind: you have said, It is not good that man should be alone; let us make to him an aid like to himself.* (Tobit 8:6). *Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore Elohim (God) hath joined together, let not man put asunder.* (Matthew 19:6). On his wedding night Tobias prays the creation back over his marriage: you made Adam and gave him Eve for a helper, and from them came mankind. When the Pharisees pressed Yahusha (Jesus) about divorce he went to the same place, to the beginning, and said that what Elohim (God) has joined no man may put asunder. The library and the gospel stand on the same ground: marriage is the Father's joining, not a human arrangement to be undone at preference. Malachi says he hates putting away (Malachi 2:16), and Tobias's prayer shows a young man who already knew it.
member_note: Tobit 8:6 — *You madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay.* The creation prayed over a marriage bed; *What therefore Elohim (God) hath joined together, let not man put asunder* (Matthew 19:6).

new_note: *And now, O Yahuah (God), I take not this my sister for lust but uprightly: therefore mercifully ordain that we may become aged together.* (Tobit 8:7). *And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.* (Malachi 2:15). Tobias tells Yahuah (God) why he is taking Sarah: not for lust but uprightly, that they may grow old together. Malachi asks why Yahuah (God) made the two one and answers it — that he might seek a godly seed — and warns the man not to deal treacherously with the wife of his youth. Tobias's prayer is that purpose spoken aloud at the start of a marriage. The seed of promise is carried through marriages entered this way, and the prophet and the young bridegroom agree on what marriage is for.
member_note: Tobit 8:7 — *I take not this my sister for lust but uprightly.* Marriage entered uprightly, for the godly seed Malachi says it was made for (Malachi 2:15).

new_note: *Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness. A little with righteousness is better than much with unrighteousness. It is better to give alms than to lay up gold:* (Tobit 12:8). *Then came to him the disciples of John, saying, Why do we and the Pharisees fast oft, but thy disciples fast not?* (Matthew 9:14). The angel Raphael tells Tobit and his son that prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness, all together, and that a little with righteousness outweighs much without it. John's disciples asked Yahusha (Jesus) why his disciples did not fast as they and the Pharisees did. He does not throw fasting out — he says the days will come when they will fast (9:15) — but he sets it where the angel set it, as one part of a life of mercy and righteousness, not a credential by itself. Fasting alone was never the discipline; fasting with prayer, alms, and righteousness is what the angel taught Tobit and what the King restores.
member_note: Tobit 12:8 — *Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness.* Fasting belongs with prayer, alms, and righteousness, not alone; the King keeps it in that place (Matthew 9:14).

new_note: *For alms does deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin. Those that exercise alms and righteousness shall be filled with life:* (Tobit 12:9). *But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* (Matthew 9:13). Raphael's last word to Tobit and Tobias is that alms deliver from death and purge away all sin, and that those who do alms and righteousness are filled with life. This is mercy given the weight of life and death. In Matthew 9 the King forgives a paralytic (9:2) and sits at table with sinners, and when the Pharisees object he sends them to Hosea: mercy, and not sacrifice. Mercy is what the Torah asked for, mercy is what delivers, and the King and the angel are saying one thing.
member_note: Tobit 12:9 — *alms does deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin.* Mercy with the weight of life and death, the mercy Hosea asked for in place of sacrifice (Matthew 9:13).
